newsitem.title: USA: It may all come down to earnings for the stock market.
newsitem.headline: It may all come down to earnings for the stock market.

text.p: Stock market investors beware. It may all come down to corporate earnings.
The experts say stocks are at a major crossroads and the greatest bull market in history could be in for another gut-wrenching drop if the upcoming round of earnings disappoint Wall Street.

This week, the Dow Jones industrial average poked its head up after being hammered down nearly 215 points in the prior week by interest-rate woes. But the market's comeback from its the fourth largest weekly point loss was short-lived.

By Friday, the index of 30 blue-chip stocks was again spinning lower as new data on inflation seemed to edge the Federal Reserve closer to another interest-rate hike after its quarter-percentage-point rise on March 25.
The Dow dropped 148.36 points Friday to 6,391.69, extending its retreat from the record close of 7,085.16 set only on March 11. For the week, it was off 134.38 points.
The concern is that 1997 may be the year of earnings accidents now that the Fed has changed its monetary course and is stepping on the interest-rate accelerator.

The latest sell-off was provoked by new government data released Friday that showed the nation's economic growth accelerated in the final three months of 1996 and that underlying inflation was showing some unwanted vitality, a likely prescription for the Fed to push interest rates higher again.

Analysts said a stock market bottom was still not at hand, and investors will be looking over their shoulders for another interest rate increase that could come as early as May 20, when the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets.
Before that happens, however, traders will have to navigate the flood of quarterly earnings that will hit the news tickers over the next couple of weeks.
Wall Street is betting that the first quarter earnings will show an increase of nearly 12 percent from the first quarter of 1996.
But there's also a consensus that the first quarter numbers will be as good as it gets for corporate earnings, and that profit growth might slow during the rest of the year.
This could be bad news for stocks, which have gotten accustomed to a steady stream of earnings improvements.
"I think this is going to be the year of earnings shortfalls and accidents," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

"The market faces significant roadblocks and a double problem because there's pressure on stock valuation due to higher interest rates and there's also a question of whether earnings will meet expectations."

The strong dollar is also giving foreign companies a pricing advantage, helping them to cut prices to get a bigger U.S. market share, which could negatively hurt the profit margins of American companies, he said.
"Even though the economy is steaming along at a very vigorous pace, I think we are in for a period of contracting profit margins and disappointing earnings," Metz said.

"I get the feeling that earnings will be lucky if they are up at all in the first quarter ... and the estimates for the full year of 8 to 14 percent profit rise seem undo-able, and the increase will likely be in a small single digit," he said.

Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call said Wall Street expects earnings for the Standard & Poor's 500 companies will grow by 11.8 percent in this year's first quarter vs. an increase of only 7.9 percent in the first quarter of 1996.

"The first quarter of last year was the second weakest quarter of this six-year earnings recovery ... and it's important to point out that the comparisons with last year's first quarter will not be a tough one," Hill said.

The first three months of 1996 reflected the damage from a strike at General Motors Corp. and one of the worse winters on record, which severely crippled the auto, home construction, entertainment, trucking and airlines industries.

"The issue now is that the first quarter might be the best that we'll have for the next quarter or two because higher interest rates may start to impact corporate profits the rest of the year," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
"The strong dollar raises a caution flag for U.S. multi-national companies which get a great deal of their earnings from overseas," he said.
Indeed, the dollar has been flying high, soaring this week to 127.16 Japanese yen, its highest level since August 1992.

Many companies will also have a tough time repeating past successes, as they start to lose the benefits of mergers and restructurings, which have brought huge jobs cuts and plant closings in past quarters.

Some of their growth have come from trailing earnings that were generated by special gains that produced a number of good innings. But now, the companies may be running out of out home runs unless they can come up with new ways to save cost.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite index sank 28.87 points to 1,206.90, and for the week, it was off 29.83 points.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 20.69 to 737.65, losing 20.25 for the week. The American Stock Exchange index was off 7.06 at 556.13, and was off 0.60 for the week.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 9.89 to 389.47, a loss of 8.55 on the week.
